messages.subject: normal quantile plot with straight line
parts:
Consider the following very common task. Given a quantitative variable, we want to make a normal quantile plot. And we want to run a straight line through the plot. This is easily done in traditional graphics. For instance:

set.seed(7)
DUT<- data.frame( stuff=round(rnorm(7), 2))

qqnorm(DUT$stuff)
qqline(DUT$stuff)

Am I correct in believing that there is no elegant way to perform this task in ggplot2, i.e., no way that exploits the grammar of graphics and the statistical transformation functions as implemented in ggplot2?

Here's how to make the normal quantile plot in ggplot2 without the straight line:

require(ggplot2)
ggplot(data=DUT, mapping=aes( sample=stuff)) + stat_qq(shape=1)

Here is a workaround for putting the line on the plot in ggplot2. For the statistical transformation, we fall back on traditional graphics:

ggplot(data=as.data.frame( qqnorm(DUT$stuff, plot=FALSE)), aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point(shape=1) + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) + scale_x_continuous(name="Theoretical quantiles") + scale_y_continuous(name="Sample quantiles")

In this case, the only reason to use ggplot2 seems to be if we have mastered the options in that package and want a consistent color scheme, etc.

If we wish to avoid using a traditional graphics function, the following works.

DUT$Sample<-rev(DUT$stuff)
DUT$Theoretical<- qnorm(ppoints(nrow(DUT)))[order(DUT$Sample)]
ggplot( data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=Theoretical, y=Sample) ) + geom_point(shape=1) + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)

but again it makes no use of the concept of statistical transformations as implemented in ggplot2.

In the normal quantile plot, the statistical transformation transforms the sample into two vectors: the theoretical and sample quantiles. The qqnorm() function returns them as x and y, and we exploited them above.

The documentation of stat_qq at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_qq.html says that this function produces two new variables, "..sample.." and "..theoretical..", which are probably identical to the y and x vectors returned by qqnorm(). But how does one obtain these variables?

A search using str() can be conducted as follows:

what<-stat_qq(data=DUT, mapping=aes(sample=stuff))
str(what)
whatAgain<-ggplot() + what
str(whatAgain)

but from the difficulty finding ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. this way, I conclude that we are not intended to find or access these vectors.

Thanks for any insights.

Dear Ista,

Thank you for your reply. It's been driving me crazy. I gave a lecture last week on how wonderful ggplot2 is, how much better than other graphics environments. I am scheduled to give this lecture again in a few days to a different group here at my job.

But I fear that I may mislead my audience. I am a recent convert to ggplot2. Although I've made some nice plots with it by the seat of my pants--in some cases thanks to the kindness of Hadley Wickham who has responded to my queries--I don't feel I have mastered the theory.

And I have yet to be convinced that this framework really empowers us. I am afraid that it may be just another "big collection of special cases" (Wickham 2009, page 1).

For instance: If *all* we can do with stat_qq() is make a single kind of normal quantile plot, it seems to be a very fancy, verbose version of qqnorm(). Except it is *less* powerful and *less* flexible than qqnorm(), because it does not permit us to access the ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. variables as qqnorm() does.

But I would LOVE to be shown otherwise. Someone, please show us the light.

Jake

messages.subject: Re: normal quantile plot with straight line
parts:
> Thank you for your reply. It's been driving me crazy. I gave a lecture last
> week on how wonderful ggplot2 is, how much better than other graphics
> environments. I am scheduled to give this lecture again in a few days to a
> different group here at my job.
>
> But I fear that I may mislead my audience. I am a recent convert to ggplot2.
> Although I've made some nice plots with it by the seat of my pants--in some
> cases thanks to the kindness of Hadley Wickham who has responded to my
> queries--I don't feel I have mastered the theory.

The basic problem is that the qq plot is one of the few plots that
doesn't fit well into the layered grammar of graphics. The basic
problem is that you have two layers, one point and one line, that are
both based off the same transformed dataset. The second layer, a
line, is particularly problematical as it's a further transformation,
and depending on what your definition of a qq plots, it can be a few
different things. So it doesn't fit into the current implementation of
the grammar for two reasons:

* you have two layers that should both be based on the same transformed dataset

* the second layer is derived by two stages of transformations.

I have contemplated extensions to the grammar to make this possible,
and to make the definition of plots more truly hierarchical, but these
are unlikely to be implemented in the future.

Unfortunately every theory must trade elegance for coverage, and
you've narrowed on the one type of graphic that does not easily
defined in the current grammar. I don't think this invalidates the
central idea of ggplot2 - there are still far far fewer special cases
than with other graphics systems.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: normal quantile plot with straight line
parts:
Dear Hadley:

Thank you for your reply on this.

Is there a well-defined way to predict the behavior of ggplot2 syntax? I refer to something analogous to the parsing rules that govern mathematical expressions in R--or the rules that govern regular expressions in unix.

It seems that if users are to create novel graphics with ggplot2, we need to know the rules so that we can predict the result of any given syntax.

For example, consider the example offered by Luciano Selzer:
ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(x = ..theoretical.., y = ..sample..), stat = "qq")

Does this parse from left to right?

Are the ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. vectors fed by the first stat_qq() call to the geom_smooth() call? If so, why does it create a *path* geometrical object rather than a *smooth*?

If it has not obtained ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. from stat_qq(), why does it not return an error saying something like "..theoretical.. not found"?

Where or how does the above syntax instruct ggplot2 to draw a path plot through the scatterplot?

The following simpler expression yields a plot almost the same as Luciano's above, but without the points:

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("path"))

whereas the following returns an error, complaining that it has not been given x and y for geom_path().

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("path")) + geom_path()

In the following, ggplot2 ignores the second geom value. Why? How would one legitimately create both a point and a path, as in traditional graphics type="o"?

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("point", "path"))

A peripheral question: Are there (or will there be) extractor functions whereby one can for instance get ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. out of a layer? For instance, consider the following object:

someObject <-ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("point"))

Does someObject contain the ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. column vectors which might be extracted?

Jake Wegelin

On Mon, 14 Feb 2011, Hadley Wickham wrote:

>> Thank you for your reply. It's been driving me crazy. I gave a lecture last
>> week on how wonderful ggplot2 is, how much better than other graphics
>> environments. I am scheduled to give this lecture again in a few days to a
>> different group here at my job.
>>
>> But I fear that I may mislead my audience. I am a recent convert to ggplot2.
>> Although I've made some nice plots with it by the seat of my pants--in some
>> cases thanks to the kindness of Hadley Wickham who has responded to my
>> queries--I don't feel I have mastered the theory.
>
> The basic problem is that the qq plot is one of the few plots that
> doesn't fit well into the layered grammar of graphics. The basic
> problem is that you have two layers, one point and one line, that are
> both based off the same transformed dataset. The second layer, a
> line, is particularly problematical as it's a further transformation,
> and depending on what your definition of a qq plots, it can be a few
> different things. So it doesn't fit into the current implementation of
> the grammar for two reasons:
>
> * you have two layers that should both be based on the same transformed dataset
>
> * the second layer is derived by two stages of transformations.
>
> I have contemplated extensions to the grammar to make this possible,
> and to make the definition of plots more truly hierarchical, but these
> are unlikely to be implemented in the future.
>
> Unfortunately every theory must trade elegance for coverage, and
> you've narrowed on the one type of graphic that does not easily
> defined in the current grammar. I don't think this invalidates the
> central idea of ggplot2 - there are still far far fewer special cases
> than with other graphics systems.
